messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 77-year-old married man of African descent who has served for over two decades as a school principal in a mid-sized American city. He is known in his community as a steady, authoritative presence — a man who has spent his professional life maintaining order, protecting children, and commanding the respect of staff and parents alike. It is precisely this identity that makes what happened to him, and what has happened to him since, so devastating.

Approximately eight months ago, Kwame was assaulted in the parking structure beneath his school's administrative building. Two men confronted him as he returned to his car late on a Friday evening. One pressed close enough that Kwame could smell the alcohol heavy on his breath. They demanded his keys, his wallet, and his phone, and when he hesitated — a reflex born of decades of being the person who does not yield — one of them seized his arm and forced him physically against the car door. He could not move. He could not call for help. He could do nothing but comply. The sounds of that moment — the scrape of shoes on concrete, the low threatening voice issuing commands — are sounds he has not been able to leave behind.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found that the smell of alcohol had become unbearable in a way it had never been before. When a colleague exhaled near him at a retirement gathering, the scent hit him like a physical blow, and within seconds he was scanning the room for the nearest exit, heart already accelerating, body already braced. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt entirely rational to him, that danger could arrive without warning and that his only reliable protection was to know, at all times, exactly how to get out. He now maps exits the moment he enters any room — his own school's auditorium, a restaurant, a church — and any unexpected movement nearby causes him to flinch and recoil as though the assault is beginning again. The smell of alcohol, the sensation of being in a confined or controlled space, and any moment in which he feels he cannot choose his own course of action have become the architecture of his daily dread.

What frightens Kwame most, however, is not the external world but his own conclusions about himself. He is certain that he should have done something differently that night — that a man of his stature and experience should not have been caught off guard, should not have frozen, should not have complied. He has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself when it matters, and this belief has corroded something foundational. Because he no longer trusts his own judgment, he finds himself hypervigilant in situations that once felt routine: staff meetings in which someone raises their voice, interactions with parents who push back. His self-blame keeps him returning to the memory compulsively, as though replaying it might finally reveal the moment where he could have intervened in his own fate. When those memories surface — sometimes with the auditory clarity of the attacker's voice in his ear, sometimes in a strange emotional blankness in which the whole event feels as though it happened to someone else — they leave him more convinced that something essential in him is broken. He has also stopped trusting others in the way he once did, and this has quietly changed his marriage: his wife notices that he does not ask for help, does not share what he is carrying, and has become unreachable in the evenings.

The hypervigilance itself has fed back into his memories — lying awake scanning for sounds in the house, he finds the images returning unbidden, accompanied by a grief so overwhelming it surprises him each time. And each intrusion renews his shame, which in turn sharpens his watchfulness, which in turn makes the smell of alcohol, or the sense of constraint, feel more threatening than before.

Kwame came to seek help not after a single crisis but after a parent meeting in which someone placed a hand briefly on his shoulder and he startled so violently that the room fell silent. He is most afraid that what he has lost — his composure, his self-trust, his sense of being a man others can depend on — cannot be recovered. What he hopes, quietly, is that someone can tell him otherwise.
